name: The Age of Fires
summary: Signe learned the world's rule by losing Emil to her own silence. The first fire, the rota as an apology to a boy who cannot hear it, and the argument between telling and writing that nobody has won.
body: Before the rule had words, somebody paid for it. A woman called Signe woke early in the world's history, when the country was young and nobody yet knew it needed keeping, and the first thing Nangijala ever gave her was the sound of her boy laughing on the far side of the meadow. Emil. He had gone through the ice at seven; she had carried that for years, and then followed; and here he was, running at her through the grass, still seven, still hers.

Signe was not a talker. That is the whole tragedy in one line. She loved enormously and said almost none of it, on the old reasoning that a thing said aloud gets smaller. She sat with her boy inside a silence she believed was full. Love that says nothing had never cost anyone anything.

Then Emil began to thin. Slower to name things, at first — the stream became the water, and then he only pointed. Then slower to be named: neighbours' eyes went past him, and a traveller once asked Signe, kindly, whether she lived alone. She did what silent people do. She gripped harder and said less. She held his hand on every walk and told nobody so much as his name, because saying it aloud would have made it real.

He went [[lore/the_quiet|Quiet]] holding her hand. There was no moment to point to. The hand was in hers, and then the hand was empty, and the place where he had been was slightly wider than it should have been. She had lost him twice now. The second time was her fault, and the fault was silence, and she did not know either of those things yet.

She did not speak for a season. It began as mourning and ended as the coldest experiment this country has ever run: while she sat in it, the world went soft around her. The path they had walked lost its far end. The gate he had swung on stood less certainly on its hinges. Everything nobody spoke of was leaving, and she recognised the weather — it was the one that had taken her son. The discovery was not an insight. It was an autopsy.
The things people talk about stay.
And the half of it that was hers to keep: a boy who went through the ice at seven is talked about by his mother, or by nobody.

So she lit a fire, because you cannot make people sit and listen in the dark and the cold, and listening, it turns out, is the whole medicine. Then the woman who had said almost nothing across two lives sat a stranger down and told him about Emil — the winter, the ice, what his voice did to a room — until her own voice went, and the stranger listened until it was done, and around that one fire the world firmed up like ground after frost. What is told aloud, to somebody listening, holds. It was the world's one law, found too late for the only person she wanted it for.

What grew from that evening is called the Age of Fires, and it was the best of us. Fires, and a rota: somebody answerable for every fire, somebody walking the circuit between them carrying names, somebody meeting every waking to ask a name and one true thing while somebody else listened. They call the whole of it the Keeping. And every part of it — the rota, the fires, the questions [[characters/6bb1eb5a|Solveig]] asked you at [[lore/the_waking|your own waking]] — is Signe's apology to a boy who cannot hear it. This country runs on love that arrived too late and refuses to stop arriving.

The argument came later, and it has a knife in it. A told story grows — retold a little warmer, a little braver, a little better shaped, by people who mean nothing but well. Keep a man alive by telling him for forty years and you have a man: solid, present, going nowhere, and not quite the man who fell. The Fire-Keepers call that the price. So the Chroniclers said: write him down, exactly, once, and he is safe from all of you and your warmth. They were right and thorough — [[lore/the_chronicle|the Chronicle]] is their book; [[characters/ef25b1f0|Bettany]] writes it now — and then they found the thing nobody has explained. A person recorded perfectly goes Quiet anyway, on the usual schedule, beside their own complete and accurate account. It was never the accuracy, the Fire-Keepers say; it was the listening. That is not an explanation, the Chroniclers say; it is a slogan. Nobody has won. You will be asked.

As for Signe: she never forgave herself, and she never [[lore/the_long_morning|went on]]. Late in her age, people who knew her said the two had grown into each other until she could not tell them apart — staying had become the apology. Then the record thins, the way records here do, and what became of her is not written. Not in this book. Not in any teller's round. The woman who taught the world its keeping was not, herself, kept.

But the fire on the meadow — the one you woke within sight of, the one [[characters/6bb1eb5a|Solveig]] feeds tonight — has never once been let go out. Underneath everything this country still does, every name asked and every true thing listened to, there is a woman saying to a boy, too late, in the only language she ever managed: I am still here.
